title: The Wilted Flower (Español)
summary: A fawning courtier claims his garden flowers never fade under Akbar's glorious reign. Birbal uses a simple bee to prick the bubble of sycophancy. [ES]
full_text:
In the court of Emperor Akbar, courtiers constantly competed to outdo one another in lavish praise and exaggerated flattery. One sycophantic noble named Mirza Kazim, hoping to win the governorship of a wealthy province, arrived at the morning assembly carrying a magnificent, dew-drenched red rose crafted with such exquisite petals that it looked like a marvel of nature.

Kazim bowed nine times and presented the blossom to Akbar: 'O Shadow of God! So blessed is your imperial reign that even the laws of decay have ceased in my gardens! This rose was plucked seven weeks ago, yet under the radiant aura of your divine justice, it refuses to wither! It remains as fresh as the moment it bloomed!'

Akbar, though wise, was intrigued by the flawless flower. 'Can this be true? Does nature herself halt her cycles in honor of our throne?'

The courtiers chorused in unison: 'Undoubtedly, Sire! The Emperor's virtue preserves all beauty!'

Birbal sat quietly in his pavilion, observing the waxy sheen along the petal edges and the stiff symmetry of the leaves. He stepped forward with a humble bow:

'Sire, Mirza Kazim's devotion is touching. Yet before we record this miracle in the imperial annals, let us consult the most impartial judges in your empire.'

Birbal gestured to an attendant in the palace garden. A moment later, the attendant brought a small bamboo cage containing three live honeybees collected from the jasmine bushes.

Birbal opened the cage door in the center of the hall. The three bees buzzed into the air. They flew past Mirza Kazim's magnificent rose without pausing for a single second, circled the hall, and flew straight out the open arched window to alight upon a tiny, wilting wild marigold growing in a crack between the marble steps outside!

Birbal smiled: 'Behold, Your Majesty. Man can carve wax, paint silk, and scent dead clay with rosewater to flatter an emperor. But the humble bee seeks only life and nectar. It knows that Mirza Kazim's rose is made of painted wax, while the wilting weed outside possesses genuine life created by the Almighty.'

Akbar examined the rose closely, felt the softening wax beneath his warm fingers, and frowned with displeasure at the fawning courtier. Mirza Kazim slunk away in disgrace, while Akbar thanked Birbal for keeping his court grounded in honesty.
